# Bhallātiyajātaka (Ja 504)

**ID:** Ja 504
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Bhallātiyajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** King Bhallātiya and the Pixies

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Bhallātiyajātaka* (Ja 504) is a canonical birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. The contemporary frame narrative (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana and centers on a dispute between King Pasenadi of Kosala and Queen Mallikā [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887; Galasek 2016]. Following a domestic quarrel regarding conjugal rights, the angry king refused to speak to her, attributing her behavior to foolish pride in the royal luxuries provided to her [SuttaCentral; Galasek 2016]. When the Buddha arrives for alms, he enquires after Mallikā's absence and reconciles the estranged couple by recounting a story of the past (*atītavatthu*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887; Galasek 2016]. In that previous life, the royal couple had lived as fairies (*kinnaras*) who spent a single night separated from each other and subsequently mourned that loss for seven hundred years [SuttaCentral; Galasek 2016; Rhys Davids 1890]. At the conclusion of the tale, the Buddha reveals the rebirths: the female fairy was Queen Mallikā, while King Bhallātiya was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1887].

V. Fausböll notes that the opening of the *Bhallātiyajātaka* exhibits marked similarity between prose and verse (*Bhallātiyo nāma ahosi rājā*), and observes that ancient stūpa reliefs label this narrative under the title *Kinnara-jātaka* [Fausböll 1897]. The text is also cited in later paracanonical Pali literature: the *Milindapañha* (Mil 7.6.9, *Sappaṅgapañha*) quotes the verse of the two fairy birds mourning their single night spent away from home against their will [SuttaCentral; Rhys Davids 1890]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations across four languages [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis in DharmaNexus shows 26 matching canonical passages (amounting to 3,750 shared characters) with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Vol. 4), and automatically aligns the text with 10 matches in the Tibetan *Vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* (*’Dul ba phran tshegs kyi gzhi*, D0006-2) [DharmaNexus].
